editorialDecisions: Do not claim the world's first military specification: British equipment records and the American A-11 predate the W.W.W.
All twelve names included. Shared requirements did not mean identical cases, movements, interchangeable components or twelve Swiss-owned factories.
Vertex had a British business background and Swiss manufacturing connections. Vertex and Timor have contemporary products and are not described as extinct.
Only IWC's own documented May-June 1945 delivery window and one Longines archive invoice of 17 July 1945 are stated; do not infer every watch's individual issue date.
The 1944 Harwell photograph illustrates the need for coordinated time. It does not identify any W.W.W. on a soldier's wrist. Hero explicitly separates 1944 and 1945.
Mark X treated as collectors' terminology, not a universal official designation. W.W.W. general-service watches distinguished from RAF Mark 11 navigation watches.
Technical requirements distinguished from delivered compliance; no blanket claim that all twelve had shock protection, all-steel cases, hacking or modern chronometer certification.
Natural Hungarian prose, equivalent English, no inline body hyperlinks and no U+2014. Sources remain in frontmatter.
Scheduling calendar review is recorded separately in docs/calendar-review-dirty-dozen-2026-10-13.json. Inaccessible sources are disclosed; no false full-radar sign-off.

evidence.source: David Read, Horological Journal, January 2022, pp.16-17
evidence.supports: R.S./Prov/4373A identifier, expanded designation, general-service role, distinction between specification and shock/corrosion performance, Malaya corrosion investigation.
evidence.publicDomainPrimaryExcerpt: The article reproduces the 1945 British government specification: minimum 15 jewels, non-magnetic lever type, overcoil, approved shock protection and testing at 32 C in four positions. These original government technical requirements are distinguished from Read's modern narrative.
evidence.caution: Do not convert the positional-rate-difference criterion to an absolute daily-accuracy guarantee. No such numerical accuracy claim included.

evidence.supports: Earlier British military timekeeping records, government markings and twelve W.W.W. suppliers.
evidence.caution: Equipment-list dates are not necessarily initial delivery dates, as the author explicitly notes.

evidence.supports: IWC calibre H/83, about 6000 watches, deliveries May-June 1945, distinction from the later RAF Mark 11.

All twelve makers and later film-derived collectors' nickname.
evidence.caution: Do not repeat the catalogue's apparent Omega calibre transcription error or turn approximate overall production numbers into exact counts.
